data.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in a month
data.description:
Google released Gemini 4 Neon today, Nov. 18, a new artificial intelligence model built for coding, knowledge work and long-running AI agents. It is rolling out in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, in Gemini for business, in Google Antigravity for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers and in the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers. Developers pay $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens.


Neon is the fourth model in Google’s Gemini 4 family, following Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen, and it arrived barely a month after the lineup began. Google is pitching it as a model people will use every day, landing between the cheaper Hydrogen and the flagship Carbon.


What can Gemini 4 Neon do?

Neon takes in text, images, video, audio and PDFs, but it only produces text. It has a context window of about 1 million tokens and supports computer use, code execution, file search and grounding through Google Search and Maps. It offers four thinking levels, so users can trade speed for deeper reasoning.

Google says Neon was built for long-running agent work involving many tools, either on its own or as an orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. A separate version, Gemini 4 Neon for cyber, is rolling out to trusted security defenders in the coming days through Google’s Fairwind Program.

Starting today, Gemini 4 Neon is available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers on mobile, desktop, and web.

This new model excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses. 🧵

— Google Gemini (@GeminiApp) November 18, 2026

How does Gemini 4 Neon perform on benchmarks?

Google’s own numbers are strong. It says Neon ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index at 58.6, first on Zapier’s AutomationBench at 56.3% and second on the Vals Index at 70.9%. Google also says Neon ranks first on Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench. The company reports a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its highest thinking level, which would place it third overall.

Context matters here. According to Artificial Analysis, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 on that index and OpenAI’s top Astra model scores 62, both above Neon, while Gemini 4 Carbon sits at 60. Google’s launch table shows Neon ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI’s Sol model on most of the tests it lists, but those numbers come from Google, and independent evaluations have not yet arrived.

Is Gemini 4 Neon actually cheaper?

It depends on how you count. Google calls Neon ‘Flash tier’ in cost, but at $3 and $15 per million tokens, it costs twice as much as Hydrogen, which runs $1.50 and $7.50. It also costs more than Carbon’s introductory price of $2 and $10, though Carbon’s rate doubles to $4 and $20 on Dec. 1.

Google’s argument is about the total bill, not the per-token rate. The company says Neon’s cost per task at the high thinking level is 32% lower than Carbon’s. Models that think longer burn more tokens, so the real cost depends on how much reasoning each job needs. For startups and independent developers watching every dollar, that difference between price per token and price per task is the number to test.

Why did Gemini 4 Neon show up before Google announced it?

Watchers spotted it early. A reference to the model appeared in the Gemini web app on Nov. 16, then in Google Cloud’s pricing catalog and in Antigravity’s command line tool on Nov. 18, before Google made it official the same day. Some had guessed Neon would be a small, budget model. It turned out to be a midweight reasoning model.

The pace is the bigger story. Google has stacked Gemini 4 releases week after week, and Neon will not be the last. Rumored names like Helix and Krypton are already circulating. The race among Google, OpenAI and Anthropic is moving faster than most businesses can test the models.

data.title: Microsoft reveals 3 causes behind massive Outlook outage
data.description:
Microsoft is finally explaining what went wrong during last week’s massive Outlook outage, which left people around the world struggling to use the popular email service across two full workdays. On Monday, November 16, a company executive apologized for the disruption in a lengthy social media post and laid out a chain of problems that combined to knock the platform offline, ABC News reported.


Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said a hidden software defect, a spike in demand and reduced server capacity all played a role in the breakdown.


A widespread disruption

The outage rippled across a wide range of industries. Businesses, government offices, schools and health care providers all reported communication problems as the email service faltered.

Other Microsoft platforms, including Teams and Xbox Live, were also affected for hours across North America, leaving many workers unable to reach colleagues or clients during the busiest part of the week.

The company had previously said the outage was not caused by a hack and that its AI agents were not responsible.

The 3 causes behind the outage

Lamanna identified three main issues that worked together to bring Outlook down.

The first was a hidden defect that had been lying dormant in the system. Under certain conditions, the bug caused servers to become overwhelmed and stop responding. According to Lamanna, the flaw came from a fix that Microsoft had prepared specifically for its Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers back in July.

The second cause was a sudden surge in traffic hitting that networking gateway, which put added pressure on the system.

The third factor was reduced server capacity. Lamanna noted that this reduction would not have caused any problems by itself, but it became significant when combined with the other two issues.

How the problems combined

When the increased traffic met the reduced capacity, the networking gateway triggered the bug that had been introduced months earlier. Requests then began piling up until the servers stopped responding altogether.

The timing made matters worse. The failure struck during the peak window of internet traffic in the United States, when demand for email and workplace tools is at its highest.

Why recovery took so long

Many users were frustrated by how long it took for service to return to normal. Lamanna explained that recovery was slower than usual because of the way the system came back online.

As servers were restored, they were immediately flooded by the backlog of waiting traffic. That sudden rush overwhelmed them again, causing them to become unresponsive and repeating the cycle. Breaking that loop took additional time, extending the outage well beyond what customers might typically expect.

Microsoft says it’s sorry

In his update, Lamanna offered a sincere apology on behalf of the company. He said Microsoft deeply regrets the impact on its customers and recognizes how much the outage interfered with their normal business operations.

The explanation offers rare insight into how a single dormant bug can spiral into a global disruption when several pressures hit at once.

What it means for users

For the millions of people who depend on Outlook and Teams every day, the outage served as a reminder of how much modern work relies on a handful of digital platforms. When those services go dark, entire offices, classrooms and hospitals can feel the effects within minutes.

The incident also comes during a period of significant change at Microsoft, which recently offered buyouts to 60,000 employees as its spending on artificial intelligence continues to grow.

Microsoft has not said whether it will make further changes to prevent a similar outage, but the detailed breakdown suggests the company is working to rebuild trust with frustrated customers.

This story was originally reported by ABC News.

data.title: 7 Proven Ways to Recover Accidentally Deleted Files Fast
data.description:
Stop saving, downloading, or installing anything on your device right now. When you delete a file, your system usually marks that storage space as available rather than erasing the data immediately, meaning your file is likely still recoverable if you act quickly.


Most accidentally deleted files turn up within the first few minutes if you look in the right places. Follow these seven steps in order, starting with the fastest, safest fixes.


1. Check your device’s trash or Recently Deleted folder

Your operating system almost always moves deleted items to a temporary holding folder first. On Windows, double-click the Recycle Bin, right-click your file and select Restore.

On Mac, open the Trash in your Dock, right-click the file and select Put Back. On iPhone and iPad, open Recently Deleted in Photos or Files and tap Recover. On Android, open Trash in Google Photos or Files by Google, tap and hold the file, and choose Restore.

2. Search your cloud storage trash and version history

If your folders sync with the cloud, deleting a file usually sends a copy to your cloud provider’s web trash bin. In Google Drive and OneDrive, open Trash or Recycle bin, right-click your file and hit Restore, within 30 days.

For iCloud Drive, open Recently Deleted at iCloud.com. If you saved over a document instead of deleting it, right-click the file in your cloud storage and select Version history.

3. Restore from a local system backup

If the trash bins are empty, your computer may have saved a background snapshot. On Windows, right-click inside the folder where the file used to live, select Properties, click the Previous Versions tab and click Restore. On Mac, click the Time Machine icon in your menu bar, scroll back in time, highlight your file and click Restore.

4. Hunt down auto-saved copies and hidden duplicates

Programs and messaging apps often leave copies behind. In Word, Excel, or PowerPoint, go to File > Info > Manage Document and select Recover Unsaved Documents.

In Google Docs or Apple Pages, check File > Version history. Search your email Sent folder, WhatsApp, Slack, Teams, and your Downloads folder, since you can download a fresh copy from any thread where you shared the file.

5. Use reputable data recovery software, carefully

When a file is emptied from the Recycle Bin, it remains on your drive until new data overwrites it. Most modern laptops use solid-state drives with a feature called TRIM, which wipes deleted data within minutes, so recovery software works best on external hard drives, SD cards, and USB flash drives.

Never install it on the drive that holds your lost file, or save recovered files back to it. Stick to reputable tools such as Windows File Recovery, Recuva, or PhotoRec.

6. Call a professional service for critical drives

If your hard drive is making clicking, grinding, or buzzing noises, or suddenly stopped showing up on your computer, unplug it immediately and do not run software scans, as a failing disk can destroy your data permanently.

Professional clean-room labs typically cost several hundred dollars, so reserve them for irreplaceable photos, legal records, or vital business files, and choose a lab that offers a free evaluation and a no data, no fee policy.

7. Set up the 3-2-1 backup rule so it never happens again

Follow the industry-standard 3-2-1 Backup Rule. Keep three copies of your data on two different storage types, such as your internal drive and an external USB drive, with one copy offsite in the cloud.

Standard cloud syncing is not a true backup, because deleting a synced file deletes it everywhere. Turn on Windows File History or Mac Time Machine, and test restoring a random file once a year.

What you should do right now

Stop downloading files or installing apps on the affected device. Check your desktop Recycle Bin or Trash and your cloud storage Trash folder immediately. Write down the exact file name, file type, and the last date you remember seeing it to make searching easier.

data.title: 7 Simple Tricks to Free Up Phone Storage Without Deleting Apps
data.description:
Seeing the Storage Almost Full warning doesn’t mean you need a new phone. Most of your missing space is likely hiding in three places: high-resolution videos, bloated messaging apps, and cached junk files you don’t even know exist.


To keep your phone running smoothly and able to install security updates, experts recommend keeping 10% to 20% of your total storage free. Follow these seven quick fixes, ordered from biggest space-savers to long-term habits, to reclaim several gigabytes in under 10 minutes.


The biggest storage hogs, and how much space you can save

Storage culprit Why it fills your phone so fast Potential space saved
4K videos and Live Photos Just 1 minute of 4K video at 60fps uses ~400 MB of space 5 GB – 50+ GB
WhatsApp and Messages Group chats auto-download every meme, voice note, and video 2 GB – 20+ GB
Social and streaming apps TikTok, Instagram, and Netflix cache huge amounts of offline data 1 GB – 15 GB
Forgotten downloads Old PDFs, zip files, and offline playlists sit untouched for years 500 MB – 5 GB

1. Check your storage breakdown first

Before deleting random apps, see exactly what is eating your space so you can target the biggest culprits first.

On iPhone: Open Settings > General > iPhone Storage. Wait a few seconds for the color-coded bar to load, then scroll down to see your apps ranked from largest to smallest.

On Android: Open Settings > Storage (or open the Files by Google app and tap Clean). You will see a clear breakdown of apps, images, videos, and system files.

2. Back up and clear heavy photos and videos (safely)

Photos and videos are the number one reason phones run out of space. A single minute of 4K video at 60 frames per second eats roughly 400 MB on an iPhone.

Back up properly: Upload your camera roll to Google Photos or iCloud Photos over Wi-Fi and confirm the backup says Complete.

Delete safely: On Google Photos, tap your profile picture and select Free up space. This safely removes local copies from your phone while keeping them in the cloud. (Warning: If you use iCloud Photos, deleting a photo from your phone also deletes it from iCloud. Instead, turn on Optimize iPhone Storage under Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Photos).

Empty the trash: Deleting photos doesn’t free up space right away. Open your Recently Deleted or Trash folder and empty it permanently.

Clean up clutter: Delete screen recordings, blurry bursts, and duplicate screenshots.

3. Trim bloated WhatsApp and messaging media

Messaging apps quietly hoard thousands of forwarded videos, GIFs, and memes in the background.

Clean WhatsApp: Open WhatsApp and go to Settings > Storage and data > Manage storage. Tap Larger than 5 MB or select your busiest group chats to bulk-delete heavy videos you no longer need. While there, turn off Media auto-download on cellular data.

Clean iPhone Messages: Go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage > Messages. Tap Review Large Attachments to wipe massive videos sent over text without deleting your actual chat history.

4. Offload unused apps without losing your data

Games, travel apps, and shopping apps frequently balloon to over 1 GB each, even if you only open them twice a year.

On iPhone: Go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage, tap an app you rarely use, and select Offload App. This deletes the heavy app software to free up space, but keeps your login details, documents, and game progress saved on your phone.

On Android: Open Settings > Apps, sort by Size, and uninstall apps you haven’t opened in the last three months.

5. Clear app caches and forgotten offline downloads

Apps like TikTok, Instagram, Chrome, and Spotify store temporary files (cache) and offline downloads that pile up over time.

Clear Android app cache: Go to Settings > Apps, select a heavy social or browser app, tap Storage & cache, and hit Clear cache. (Do not tap Clear storage/data, as that will log you out).

Clear iPhone browser and app cache: Open Settings > Safari and tap Clear History and Website Data. For bloated social apps like TikTok or Snapchat, open the app’s internal settings to clear its cache, or delete and reinstall the app.

Wipe offline media: Open Netflix, YouTube, Spotify, or Apple Podcasts and delete downloaded movies, playlists, and episodes you have already finished.

6. Move large files to the cloud or an external drive

If you have work documents, raw videos, or massive zip files sitting in your phone’s Downloads folder, move them off your device.

Use free cloud storage: Google gives you 15 GB free (shared across Drive, Gmail, and Photos), while Apple gives 5 GB free with iCloud. Paid upgrades start around $1 to $3 a month if you need extra room.

Plug in external storage: If you have an iPhone 15 or newer (with USB-C) or almost any Android phone, you can plug a USB-C flash drive directly into your charging port and transfer large videos off your phone in seconds. Many Android phones also support microSD cards for cheap, permanent storage expansion.

7. Change three settings to stop your phone from filling up again

Once your space is back, tweak a few default settings so you don’t end up right back here next month:

Lower your video resolution: Go to your Camera settings and switch video recording from 4K down to 1080p HD at 30fps. It looks great on phone screens and uses a fraction of the space.

Auto-delete old texts: On iPhone, go to Settings > Messages > Keep Messages and change it from Forever to 1 Year or 30 Days. In WhatsApp, turn on Disappearing Messages for noisy group chats.

Enable auto-offloading: Turn on Offload Unused Apps under Settings > App Store (iPhone) or Auto-archive apps in the Google Play Store settings (Android).

What you should do right now

Open your phone’s Storage screen to spot your #1 space hog.

Delete your 3 largest videos or clear your WhatsApp media, then empty your Recently Deleted folder.

Restart your phone. A quick reboot clears out temporary system files and often frees up an extra 1 GB to 2 GB automatically.

data.title: China warns U.S. against new Nvidia chip restrictions
data.description:
China is urging the United States against introducing additional restrictions on semiconductor exports, as a growing controversy involving Nvidia and its former chief executive, Jensen Huang, draws attention to the country’s technology trade with Beijing.


The Chinese government reiterated its opposition to expanded export controls Friday, Nov. 13, arguing that additional restrictions could disrupt international manufacturing networks and commercial relationships.


The statement comes as U.S. lawmakers consider tighter limits on technology shipments to China following questions about Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chip sales and the federal government’s oversight of those transactions.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning addressed the issue during a regular briefing in Beijing. She emphasized China’s position that export restrictions should not be used in ways that interfere with international supply chains or commercial cooperation.

Beijing also called for Washington to maintain stable economic and trade relations between the two countries, pointing to previous discussions between their respective leaders.

Nvidia controversy puts semiconductor exports under scrutiny

The diplomatic exchange follows the departure of Huang from Nvidia, which became a major development in the ongoing controversy surrounding the technology company.

Huang resigned Thursday, Nov. 12, after acknowledging an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore based data center company Megaspeed. The two individuals are not related.

The circumstances surrounding the relationship have also drawn attention to questions about the federal government’s handling of Nvidia‘s business dealings involving China.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced scrutiny over his professional connections to Chinese companies and his friendship with Huang. Critics have questioned whether those relationships affected the Commerce Department’s oversight of billions of dollars in Nvidia artificial intelligence chip sales.

The department had not responded to a request for comment on the matter as of Friday.

Bessent indicated that the Treasury Department, Defense Department, State Department and U.S. trade representative had supported placing the Singapore based company on the federal government’s Entity List.

The designation is significant because companies included on the list face restrictions on accessing certain U.S. technology products and services.

Bessent said the agencies had supported the proposed designation for months, while responsibility for the final decision rested with the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security.

Lutnick expected to appear before Senate committee

The dispute has also drawn congressional attention, with lawmakers examining how federal agencies handled decisions involving semiconductor exports and companies operating in the international technology market.

According to a U.S. official, Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10.

His expected appearance could provide lawmakers with an opportunity to examine the Commerce Department’s internal procedures and its decisions concerning Megaspeed.

House Speaker Mike Johnson has also indicated that support is growing in Congress for additional restrictions on semiconductor exports to China.

The discussions reflect broader concerns in Washington about China’s access to advanced computing technology and the potential implications for the U.S. technology industry.

Intelligence reports add another dimension

The controversy has also been shaped by intelligence related reporting involving Alice Huang.

The New York Times reported Oct. 29 that President Donald Trump had received information approximately a year earlier suggesting that Alice Huang was connected to Chinese intelligence and had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang.

According to the publication, Trump decided against taking action based on the information presented to him.

A separate New York Times report published Nov. 6 detailed a government memorandum circulated the previous spring. The document reportedly referenced intelligence suggesting Alice Huang was working on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security, the country’s principal intelligence organization.

The claims have added another layer to the questions surrounding Nvidia, its leadership and the movement of advanced technology between the United States and China.

Beijing has rejected the allegations. Chinese officials have characterized the claims as an attempt to justify restrictions intended to limit the country’s technological development, particularly its progress in artificial intelligence.

U.S. China technology relations remain a central issue

China’s latest statement highlights the continuing disagreement between Washington and Beijing over access to advanced semiconductor technology.

The United States has increasingly relied on export restrictions as part of its approach to limiting China’s access to certain advanced computing products and manufacturing equipment.

These measures have become a significant issue for technology companies operating across international markets, particularly those involved in artificial intelligence development.

For China, additional restrictions could affect access to essential components used in advanced computing systems. For U.S. policymakers, the debate involves technology exports, national security considerations and the oversight of companies conducting business internationally.

With congressional scrutiny continuing and Lutnick’s scheduled testimony approaching, the Nvidia controversy is likely to remain part of the broader discussion over semiconductor trade and U.S.- economic relations.

data.title: Google says no evidence of widespread Gmail outage
data.description:
Gmail users flooded outage trackers with complaints on Tuesday, but Google says it isn’t seeing signs of a widespread problem.


The tech giant said on Tuesday, November 17, that it had found no evidence of a broad disruption to its popular email service, even as thousands of people reported trouble with their inboxes.


Thousands of users reported problems

By noon ET, outage tracking website Downdetector had logged more than 2,800 reports of issues with Gmail. Most users said they were having trouble receiving emails, while others reported problems getting into the service at all.

The complaints marked a second wave of reports. Downdetector data showed problems had already peaked around 2:40 p.m. ET on Monday before climbing again Tuesday morning.

For many people, Gmail is central to both work and personal life, so even scattered issues can cause headaches, from missed meeting invites to delayed verification codes and receipts.

What Google has said

A Google spokesperson told Rolling Out that the company was not seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption. The spokesperson added that Google’s teams keep a close eye on service health and that real-time updates are always available on the Google Workspace Status Dashboard.

Google shared a similar message in a post on X from its News from Google account, encouraging users to check the dashboard for the latest information. The dashboard tracks the health of Gmail along with other Workspace apps, such as Google Drive and Google Meet.

As of 1:45 p.m. ET, the dashboard did not list any active Gmail disruptions.

The gap between user complaints and Google’s assessment is worth noting. Downdetector tracks reports submitted by users, so a spike signals that many people are noticing problems, but it doesn’t necessarily mean the service is down for everyone. Issues can also stem from individual accounts, devices, internet connections or the providers sending the messages.

A week of tech failures

The Gmail reports follow a rough stretch for some of the country’s biggest systems. In recent days, Americans have dealt with several major disruptions.

  1. A Microsoft Outlook outage last week left users without email for nearly 24 hours.
  2. A telecommunications failure prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to temporarily halt flights nationwide beginning Friday, November. 13.
  3. Chase customers reported login and account problems on Monday.
  4. Marriott’s website and app saw a spike in problem reports Tuesday morning, with hundreds of users reporting trouble with logins and reservations.

Taken together, the incidents have left many people frustrated with the reliability of the digital services they depend on every day. Still, there is no evidence that the Gmail complaints are connected to any of them.

We want to be clear that we aren’t currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption, and you can always check real-time status on our Status Dashboard: https://t.co/hXJj1ijxrA

— News from Google (@NewsFromGoogle) November 17, 2026

What to do if Gmail isn’t working

If emails aren’t showing up, there are a few simple steps worth trying.

Start by checking the Google Workspace Status Dashboard to see whether the company has flagged a problem. If nothing is listed, try opening Gmail on a different device or switching between the app and a web browser, since issues sometimes affect one but not the other.

It’s also a good idea to check your spam and other folders, along with any filters you’ve set up, in case messages are being sorted somewhere unexpected. Sending a test email to yourself can show whether messages are coming through. Refreshing the page, updating the Gmail app or restarting your device can also help clear up minor glitches.

Anyone expecting time-sensitive emails may want to give contacts a heads-up or use another way to stay in touch until the issue clears up.

data.title: ARC Raiders patch fixes 50+ bugs, but these 7 remain
data.description:
ARC Raiders Live Update 2.6.0 is now live. Embark Studios brought back the Cold Snap Major Map Condition, added the Outlaw Stencil set for weapon customization and shipped a long list of fixes. The studio also says it is finishing a new project that arrives next week.


What is new in Update 2.6.0?

Cold Snap returns to the Major Map Condition rotation. The Outlaw Stencil set gives players a new way to customize weapons. Embark removed the Beachcombing Minor Map Condition from Riven Tides and expanded the mechanic to all maps.


The Dockmaster’s Detector can now find buried items everywhere except Pendola Pass, where the Mountaineer’s Detector is still required.

Live Update 2.6.0 has landed Topside, bringing a flurry of fixes and improvements to keep your runs smooth – and the Outlaw Stencil set to spruce up your hard-earned weapons.

Read the patch notes here: https://t.co/UeJnKzGjNY https://t.co/n1UsNx7D7h

— ARC Raiders (@ARCRaidersGame) November 17, 2026

What changed on the maps?

Lighting and atmosphere in Spaceport were refined to improve visibility between interiors and exteriors, with less harsh contrast and faster exposure adaptation. Buried City got better visibility in dark interiors, less cloud shadowing and subtle bloom changes.

Collision problems were fixed across Pendola Pass, Spaceport and Riven Tides. Players can now shoot through the railyard windows on Pendola Pass, and a gap behind a cliff where players got stuck was closed. Collision near the Seed Vault Airshaft in Stella Montis was also improved.

Which gameplay bugs were fixed?

Players no longer appear invisible after quickly entering and leaving a Gondola. The Road Warrior skill can recycle Weapon Amplification Modules and Candleberries during raids. Vaulting no longer drains jump stamina, and the Vaults on Vaults on Vaults skill uses none.

Players stay in place during a knockout animation, and a defibrillator revive now prevents an immediate knockout. The Hydra now aims only some weapons at Lure Grenades while still shooting at players. Firework Boxes now delay launches instead of fizzling when many are activated, and Grapple Hook lines cancel correctly if a player is downed.

What weapon changes are included?

The Stiletto’s weight drops from 7 to 6. Aiming down sights with scoped weapons no longer shifts aim sideways. A crosshair issue when moving sideways while aiming at an ARC was fixed. The Snap Hook description now shows its correct 18-meter range.

What interface and progression fixes are included?

Players can now drop items by dragging them outside the inventory. The Outpost can be upgraded to Level 4 after a bug blocked some players. Fixes cover the Ping Wheel getting stuck, Inventory bumper navigation, the Repair button and gamepad looting that could delete items. Quests that could soft lock if an item was lost are fixed. A new Times Revived By A Stranger stat appears in the Codex.

What known issues remain?

Supply drops from the Deep-Space Telescope in Pendola Pass may land out of bounds. The key room in Cielo Sereno Observatory may stay closed after using a key during the ARC Frigate condition.

Vaulting on an ARC Reclaimer can push players off, and players can get stuck in an ARC Turbine as it takes off. A tree near the Water Treatment Control building on Dam Battlegrounds can trap players. Some players cannot finish the When Everything Falls quest.

What is not confirmed?

Embark has not said what the new project arriving next week is. Sources describe a few fixes with slightly different wording, such as the invisibility bugs.

data.title: Alarming cyberattack hits 178 sites, including Zoom and CNN
data.description:
Visitors to some of the internet’s most popular websites may have been exposed to hackers looking to steal their personal and financial information.


Malicious code was planted on websites belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, HSBC and IKEA, according to cybersecurity firm Report URI. Its researchers uncovered the attack on Monday, November 16. Other affected names included Salesforce, Equifax, Fox News, Alaska Airlines and GitLab.


The software was built to grab credit card details, reroute cryptocurrency payments and target certain iPhones and iPads. It’s still unclear how many people, if any, had their information stolen.

How the attack happened

Instead of breaking into each organization one by one, the hackers went after a single shared tool. They exploited a weakness in Optimizely, a company whose software lets businesses test different versions of their websites, such as new page layouts or features.

Because so many major companies rely on that service, tampering with it allowed the attackers to slip malicious code onto the websites that used it. That meant people could encounter the harmful software just by loading an affected page.

Optimizely said in a status update on its website on Tuesday that it had fixed the problem and removed the malicious code.

What the code was designed to do

Researchers found the code could carry out several kinds of theft. One method swapped out cryptocurrency wallet addresses that users had copied, which could send payments to the hackers instead of the intended recipients.

The software could also try to steal credit card numbers, pull information saved in web browsers and take screenshots. Some of the code went after iPhones and iPads running older versions of Apple’s operating systems, trying to take advantage of known weaknesses.

In total, Report URI identified 188 affected website scripts across the 178 organizations. Researchers also traced roughly $7,040 in cryptocurrency payments to wallets tied to the attack on Nov. 16, though the full financial damage remains unknown.

The findings don’t necessarily mean hackers broke directly into all 178 companies or stole data from everyone who visited their sites.

Which organizations were affected

The list spans nearly every industry. Banking and finance took the biggest hit, with 32 organizations affected, including several regional HSBC sites, Equifax, Paychex and TaxAct. Technology accounted for 23 names, among them Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, Bitly and Optimizely itself.

Retailers such as IKEA, ASOS, Mattel, American Eagle and several regional Levi’s sites were also caught up, along with streaming services like Peacock and Starz and news outlets including CNN, the BBC, Fox News and NPR.

Other affected names ranged from KLM and Alaska Airlines to Starbucks Canada, Change.org, UNICEF USA and Mint Mobile. Report URI noted that additional organizations may have been affected beyond those it identified.

How to protect yourself

Anyone who visited an affected website on Nov. 16 should be aware of the potential risks, especially if they entered payment details or sent cryptocurrency. Still, simply opening a website does not mean information was taken.

Here are five steps to take now.

  1. Update your iPhone, iPad and other devices with the latest security updates.
  2. Check your bank accounts for unfamiliar charges, particularly if you entered card details on an affected site.
  3. Review any cryptocurrency transfers to confirm they reached the correct wallet.
  4. Watch for unexpected login alerts or changes to your online accounts.
  5. Contact your bank right away if you spot an unauthorized payment.

Investigators have not yet determined how many people may have been affected.

Source: Newsweek, originally reported by Chris Matthews.

data.title: Microsoft Outlook outage hits UK and US users: Latest updates
data.description:
Microsoft Outlook is down for thousands of users today. The company says it is investigating problems accessing Exchange Online mailboxes and that the issue may affect Microsoft 365 connectivity in any region.


What is happening with Outlook?

Users report that Outlook fails to load, shows a blank inbox or will not send emails. Many see a Failed to fetch error, which appears when a browser sends a request to a server and gets no reply. Reports of problems began in the US around 4 p.m. and in the UK just after 5:20 p.m.


We’re investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.

— Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026

How many people are affected?

Counts differ by source and time. Outage tracker Downdetector showed more than 3,300 UK reports within about 20 minutes, around 60,000 in the US, and other reports cited 39,000 or even nearly 150,000. These numbers change quickly and are user-submitted.

What has Microsoft said?

The company said it is investigating reports of users having trouble accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. It later said the issue may affect Microsoft 365 connectivity for users in any region. More details are posted in the Microsoft 365 admin center under incident EX1550543. Some users said the admin center was also hard to reach, and the company has not given a fix time.

Are Teams and Copilot affected?

Reports conflict. One outlet says hundreds of UK users had trouble with Teams and Copilot, while another says Teams was not affected, though Copilot showed a spike in reports.

What can you do?

There is no confirmed fix on the user side. Check Microsoft’s 365 status account for updates, try again later and avoid repeatedly resubmitting important emails until service returns.

What is not confirmed?

The cause of the outage and the time of the fix are unknown. One article carries an October date for a similar event, so it may describe an earlier outage. Report counts differ by source.

data.title: Stephanie Humphrey on how to give this season without falling for a holiday scam
data.description:
Stephanie Humphrey spent years as a systems engineer before she turned to helping everyday people use technology with confidence. Known online as TechLifeSteph, she is a consumer technology journalist and broadcast personality whose advice has reached viewers of Good Morning America, GMA3, CNN and Fox 29.


This time of year, her focus is scams. As holiday shopping, travel, deliveries and charitable giving pick up, so do the schemes built to empty bank accounts. The FBI reported $16.6 billion in consumer losses to internet crime in 2024, a 33% jump from the year before.


What got you into tech?

I am a former engineer by education and training. I have two engineering degrees. I worked as an engineer for a number of years, and so this has always been my life. I’m happy now to be able to use different platforms like this, right here on Rolling Out, to help people understand how technology can make their lives easier.

What is the most common holiday scam you’ve seen?

I think for the holidays, we’re going to see a lot of charity scams, because this is the time of year when people tug on those heartstrings. And not just organizational charity scams, but those folks on TikTok with the GoFundMes for their families and things like that.

I’m not saying that we shouldn’t give, because that is what we are called to do, but we have to use a little discernment in researching organizations and really paying attention to where we’re putting our money.

How can you tell when a website is a scam?

You’ve got to pay really close attention to misspellings on the site, typos and things that don’t look right. I know AI is making it really easy to clone websites so they look exactly like the site, but the URL is always going to be a little bit different, because you can’t have the same web address as a legitimate site. So you’ve got to really scrutinize the URL when you’re doing your web surfing.

That’s something a service like Xfinity Shield can help with, because the CyberSecure part of Xfinity Shield does that work for you and alerts you if a website seems malicious. It gets it before you even start clicking and downloading.

How can we keep our elderly parents safe this season?

It’s tough. I go through this with my mom as well. Number one, you have to be patient. They didn’t grow up with this technology. It’s not inherent to how they’re used to operating. I know it’s hard, but you’ve got to be a little bit patient. Walk them through different things.

In addition to protecting your Wi-Fi itself, you can set some family settings in Xfinity Shield that help them. You can block websites, and you can control the content they might have access to right in the app.

But one good tip I tell everybody, especially when it comes to those tech scams where they tell you your grandkid has been kidnapped, have a family code phrase. My family has a code phrase that only we know. Literally, me, my brother and my mom know this phrase. We say it to each other all the time. It’s been an inside joke in our family for a really long time.

Especially with those voice scams, because AI can actually clone my voice and call my mother and say, “Hey, Mom, I’m on the side of the road. My car got in an accident.” Have a family code phrase, not just a code word, because a word is easy to figure out. Then you can ask the person on the other end of the line, “What’s our code phrase?” If they don’t know it, you know it’s a scam.

What should you do in the first hour after you realize you’ve been scammed?

Depending on how much access you’ve given the scammer, number one, shut your bank accounts down, put flags on your credit cards and put holds on all of your financial accounts. Call your bank, call your credit card company and let them know, “I think I’ve been scammed. Freeze everything.” That’s the first thing.

Then you want to go into all of your accounts and change those passwords. If you’re smart with your tech, you should have a password manager that can help make that a little bit easier, so all your passwords are stored, safe and strong.

Again, you’re going to use something like Xfinity CyberSecure to run a diagnostic to make sure that nothing else in your home has been compromised. It’s not just your computer and your smartphone that are connected to your internet. Your TV, your smart speakers, some people’s refrigerators are smart. Any device in your house that has an internet connection is connected to that Wi-Fi, and it needs to be protected as well.

Is Xfinity easy to use for someone who isn’t tech savvy?

So easy to use, because number one, it’s already included. If you’re already an Xfinity customer and you have the advanced Xfinity Gateway, their upgraded router, Xfinity Shield is already in there. There’s not a whole lot you need to do, because as soon as you connect your devices to your Wi-Fi at home, they’re already covered and protected by CyberSecure.

Then you download the app, and now you have CyberSecure and the family settings in there as well. You can control screen time for your kids and block some websites if you need to. You’re going to be able to manage all of that right within the app.

How do people get started?

Just head to xfinity.com and search for Xfinity Shield, and all the info is right there.

Where can people find you?

You can find me all around the web at @techlifesteph, or you can visit my website at stephaniehumphrey.com.

What is one thing people can do right now to be more secure?

You should have two-factor authentication enabled on every single account. That’s where you log in and they text you a code and you’ve got to put the code in. It’s an extra step, I know, but it does still help. It’s not foolproof, but it does still help keep your account secure. So put that two-factor authentication in place.
